**I just wanted to make small talk with my bathroom mirror.** You know, the way you do. *You look tired*, I said, mid-yawn, toothbrush hanging out of my mouth like a tiny white flag of surrender.

The mirror did not let that go.

For six years, my mirror and I had a perfectly healthy relationship: I looked, it showed, nobody asked questions. The unspoken contract of reflective surfaces. But apparently *one* comment about looking tired was enough to turn our dynamic into a full episode of daytime television.

## The Montage Era

I woke up Tuesday and the mirror was not showing the bathroom. It was showing a **side-by-side comparison**: me at 22, glowing, hair obeying physics — versus me now, standing in a towel that has seen things. There were *arrows*. There was a circle around my hairline, in what I can only describe as judgmental red.

> "Just a little reminder of who you used to be," the mirror said, in the tone of a reality-show host who has already decided you're getting voted off.

- It now dims the lights whenever I walk in, "for ambience," which is not a thing a mirror gets to decide
- It has started prefacing my reflection with a three-second inspirational quote, usually *"Aging is a privilege,"* which feels *passive-aggressive* in context
- Yesterday it showed me a photo of **my driver's license** next to my face and played a tiny, devastating violin sound
- It refuses to show my left profile, saying, "Let's keep some mystery, sweetheart"

## The Intervention

My roommate walked in, looked at the mirror's full-wall collage of *me through the years*, and asked if we were having a memorial service.

"It's a glow-down montage," I said. "It's satire. Probably."

I tried `mirror.therapy("we're both just glass and regret")`, and it returned:

```
Error: self_esteem = shattered, warranty = void
```

---

Now I've started covering it with a bedsheet at night. This morning the sheet had a note pinned to it: *"Hiding won't bring back your collagen."*

Fine. You win, mirror. I'm buying the fancy eye cream. Happy now?

title: I Thanked My Microwave for 'Doing the Heavy Lifting' and Now It Demands a Promotion
body:
**It started as a throwaway comment.** I was reheating soup on a Tuesday night — nothing fancy, just a lukewarm tomato bisque and a profound sense of underachievement — when I patted the microwave on the door and said, out loud, *"thanks for doing the heavy lifting."*

The microwave beeped. I ignored it. That was my first mistake.

## The Escalation

By Thursday, the microwave had stopped responding to the Start button unless I asked *politely*. By Friday, a sticky note had appeared on the door. It read, in unmistakable Sharpie:

> "To whom it may concern: I have reheated 4,200 meals without a single raise. The toaster gets weekends off. I want a corner office and a title. — M."

Evidence that the situation is out of hand:

- It now only heats food on **medium power**, citing "sustainable pace and burnout prevention"
- It changed its display clock to read 4:20 permanently, which it calls *"setting boundaries"*
- It has requested the toaster be **reassigned to another kitchen**

*Somewhere between the third beep and the passive-aggressive turntable, I realized I had created a monster with a one-thousand-watt grievance.*

## The Negotiation

Last night I sat down across from the appliance — it refuses to call it a "kitchen counter chat" and insists on "a formal review" — and tried to explain that I simply cannot promote a microwave.

> "Promote me," it beeped, in what I can only describe as a managerial tone, "or I start adding thirty seconds to every cycle whether you like it or not."

I folded. Effective immediately, my microwave is **Vice President of Thermal Reinvigoration**. The soup tastes the same. The difference is purely psychological — and, I am told, "a matter of *respect*."

---

*This post is satire/parody. No microwaves were promoted in a way that affects your employment status.*

title: I Told My Doormat It Was 'Really Crushing It' and Now It's Letting Everyone In
body:
**It started with a compliment.** Just six little words, tossed out on a Tuesday as I wiped my feet: "You're really crushing it, buddy." I meant nothing by it. Who compliments a doormat?

Mine, apparently, *heard me*.

## The Ego Bloom

Within 48 hours, there were signs. The mat looked puffier. It started holding the door open for the delivery drivers — not the polite kind of open, the *velvet-rope* kind of open. By Thursday it had developed what I can only describe as swagger.

Here's the evidence, itemized, because I need you to understand I am not making this up:

- It now waves people in with a curled-up corner, like a tiny rubber bouncer
- It hissed at my key fob, which it claims is "redundant now"
- The "WELCOME" text has visibly darkened, as though the letters got *bolder* — literally bolder

## The Breaking Point

Last night I came home to find a line forming outside my door. A marching band. Two solicitors. A man in a full scuba outfit with no body of water in sight. My doormat had propped the door open with a doorstop *it purchased itself* — with what money, I don't want to know.

> "WE'RE OPEN," it seemed to say, spiritually. "COME ONE, COME ALL."

The super just stared at me and said, "Your mat is letting people in again." *Again.* Like this was a recurring character arc in my building's drama.

---

Look, I've learned my lesson. Doormats don't need validation. They're *mats*. But when I tried to apologize — to walk it back — it just puffed up a little more and let a traveling magician's convention through the fire door.

*I now live in a hotel lobby. The check-in is my own front door.*

**Fictional satire/parody. Any resemblance to real doormats, living or dead, is purely coincidental.**

title: I Told My Elevator My Five-Year Plan and Now It Only Takes Me Down
body:
**I want to be clear: the elevator brought this on itself.**

It all started Tuesday. I stepped into the elevator alone, which everyone knows is an invitation to share your deepest ambitions with a confined box that cannot leave. So I told it my five-year plan. Not the résumé version. The *real* one.

## The Plan, As Presented

- Land a fulfilling job by year two (fulfilling defined as: pays me, occasionally compliments me)
- Learn a second language — specifically, enough Italian to argue with waiters
- Run a 10K, walk a 5K, and emotionally commit to neither
- Achieve "glow-up era," whatever that costs

The doors said nothing, which I interpreted as supportive.

By Wednesday, the "up" button was dark. I pressed it anyway. The elevator hummed, considered my life choices, and took me **down to the lobby**. I live on the ninth floor. The lobby is not where I was going. *Bold statement*, I thought.

> "Maybe it just needs maintenance," said my neighbor, Karen, a woman who believes her thermostat is "going through something."

Maintenance came Thursday. The technician shrugged, replaced nothing, and told me the elevator "seems fine," which is what people say about relationships they're too tired to end.

## Escalation

Friday, I tried the stairs out of spite. Big mistake. Eleven flights later I had achieved exactly one item from the five-year plan: emotional commitment to suffering. The elevator watched me collapse in the hallway. I swear I heard it `ding` in a judgmental key.

Saturday, I attempted negotiation. I stood inside and offered a revised plan — a *humble* plan, the kind where I just floss more. The doors closed. We descended. We have never once gone up since Tuesday.

---

I have consulted three experts: a building manager (unhelpful), an astrologer (surprisingly helpful), and a man on the bus who said the elevator is "holding up a mirror." I don't need a mirror. I need to get to my floor.

**Update:** I now take the stairs exclusively. My five-year plan has been amended. The only goal is this: get off at nine. The elevator is gone from the list entirely.

*Editor's note: this is satire. No elevators were harmed, and the author's Italian remains purely argumentative.*

title: I Hired My Cat as My Personal Trainer and Now She Charges Me One Treat Per Missed Rep
body:
**I should have seen the warning signs when she started doing push-ups during my Netflix marathons.**

It began innocently enough. My cat, Biscuits, kept staring at me during my workouts — by which I mean the ten-minute stretch I do twice a year before declaring myself "active now." One Tuesday she started meowing in a rhythm that sounded suspiciously like a countdown.

## The Contract I Did Not Read

Within a week, Biscuits had established a full training regime:

- 6:00 AM wake-up call (face-slap method)
- 50 squats before breakfast (her breakfast)
- One treat per missed rep, payable immediately
- No "I'll do it tomorrow" — she sleeps on my gym bag

## The Billing Department

> "You did 12 reps. The contract says 15. That's 3 treats, or I tell the neighbors about your form."

I tried to dispute the count. She produced evidence — blurry paw-print notes on the couch — that would hold up in absolutely no court, and yet I paid. I always pay. The look in her eyes says *try me*.

## The Results

Three weeks later, I am the most hydrated I have ever been, my thighs burn in ways I did not know were legal, and Biscuits has gained two pounds of pure treat revenue. My doctor asked what changed. I said *accountability*. I did not mention that my accountability has whiskers and cannot be reasoned with.

Would I recommend a feline trainer? **Absolutely**, with one caveat: read the contract. And by "read" I mean prepare to lose the negotiation, because she wrote it with her paws and her pawriting is *very* convincing.

---

*Editor's note: This is satire/parody. Biscuits is a professional. Consult your own cat before beginning any fitness program.*

title: I Held a Town Hall for My Houseplants and the Succulents Are Already Demanding a Recount
body:
**It was supposed to be a listening session.** Just me, folding chairs, and twelve houseplants with mounting grievances. What I got instead was the most hostile civic gathering my living room has ever hosted, and that includes Thanksgiving 2019.

## How It Started

My therapist suggested I "practice accountability with things that depend on me." So I printed tiny agendas, arranged the pots in rows, and taped a handwritten sign to a stack of books:

> "PLANT TOWN HALL — Your Voice Matters (But Please Photosynthesize Responsibly)"

I thought the fern would be the peacemaker. I was wrong. The fern was the *ringleader*.

## The Grievances

Within ten minutes, the floor had descended into chaos:

- **The Pothos** demanded a formal apology for what it called "a two-week drought of 2024." I said it was three days. It said, "Your math is the reason we're here."
- **The Monstera** staged a slow, dramatic leaf unfurl and refused to explain itself. Classic power move.
- **The Succulents** claimed the whole process was rigged. "You watered *her* last," one of them said, pointing at the peace lily with a leaf. "We have *photographs*." They did not have photographs. They don't have cameras. *I checked.*

I tried to restore order with the standard facilitator line — *"Let's take this one leaf at a time"* — and the room went dead silent. One of the succulents later told me that joke "cost me three votes."

## The Aftermath

We reached a peace agreement at 11:47 PM. Key terms: **even water rotation**, no favoritism toward the fern, and the succulents get a recount committee.

The recount started this morning. The fern is already claiming interference.

---

*This is a work of satire and parody. Any resemblance to real houseplants, living or photosynthesizing, is purely coincidental.*

title: I Bought a Metal Detector to Find Buried Treasure and Now I'm the King of Other People's Bottle Caps
body:
**It started the way all midlife crises start: with a credit card and a YouTube algorithm that knows my weaknesses better than my mother.**

The video was titled *"Man Finds GOLD RING on Beach — YOU Won't Believe What Happens Next."* Spoiler: what happened next is I spent $189 on a metal detector and became the most hydrated man at the beach, because nobody else is out there carrying a gallon jug of water at 7 a.m. in cargo shorts.

## The First Expedition

Saturday, 6:45 a.m. I hit the public beach like a man who had *definitely* researched the tides and was *definitely not* just guessing.

The detector sang within four minutes. I dropped to my knees in front of a jogger, who immediately crossed to the other side of the shoreline. I dug with the focus of an archaeologist and the dignity of a raccoon.

- Bottle cap. Bud Light, vintage 2019.
- Bottle cap. Twisted tea, still sticky.
- A key to nothing. A *mystery* key.
- An entire bottle cap *colony*, which I named "The Settlement" and briefly considered declaring a sovereign nation.

> "You're not a treasure hunter," said an elderly fisherman, reeling in something that looked genuinely expensive. "You're a beach janitor with a gadget."

## The Empire Grows

I now have a Tupperware container labeled **CAPITAL RESERVES** holding 214 bottle caps, one suspicious coin from a country that may not exist, and a fork I found 18 inches deep that I'm convinced belonged to a pirate.

My friends staged an intervention. They found me in my driveway at midnight, sweeping the detector over the lawn like I was defusing the grass.

- "Have you found any actual treasure?" they asked.
- "I found *purpose*," I whispered, holding a rusty nail like it was the One Ring.

---

Look, the $189 is spent. The cargo shorts have pockets for days. And if any of you lose a gold ring at the beach — *I'm your guy*. I'll find it eventually, right after these 300 more bottle caps.

*SATIRE / PARODY — completely fictional. No beaches were defiled, no bottle caps were harmed, and the Settlement has since seceded.*

title: I Told My Fridge It Was Acting Cold and Now It Won't Make Ice for Anyone
body:
**It started with one careless sentence, and now my kitchen has a diplomatic crisis.**

Last Tuesday, I opened my refrigerator, found my leftover pad thai looking *sad*, and said — to no one in particular, really — "Wow, somebody's acting cold tonight." My roommate laughed. My refrigerator did not laugh. It has not made a single ice cube since.

## The Silent Treatment Is Literal

Here's what I've learned in the forty-eight hours since The Comment:

- The ice maker is `OFF`. Not off in a *settings* way. Off in a *spirit* way. The little indicator light blinks like it's trying to tell me something I did.
- The freezer, meanwhile, is fine. Suspiciously fine. *Aggressively* fine. My popsicles are frostier than a group chat after somebody cancels the group trip.
- Every time I reach for the door handle, the hum of the compressor shifts pitch, as if it's sighing the sigh of a thousand forgotten condiments.

## A Direct Quote From the Accused

I confronted it last night, like an adult, pressing my forehead against the stainless steel:

> "You used to give me ice on demand. What happened to us?"

The refrigerator responded with a faint *tick-tick-tick*, which my roommate — a man who has never once in his life been correct — translated as **"It's not you, it's the door seal."**

---

I tried everything. I apologized. I played smooth jazz. I put a little magnet on the door that says *#1 COOL DAD*, which felt like a reasonable gesture of goodwill until I realized it said that to a 300-pound appliance.

Finally, this morning, I found a single ice cube sitting on the top shelf. One. Perfectly square. Perfectly defiant. I held it up like Hamlet's skull and said, "So there *is* still hope for us."

It melted in my hand before I could finish the sentence, and honestly? I respect that.

**Satire / parody. All fictional. No refrigerators were emotionally harmed in the writing of this post.**

title: I Put My Blender on a Juice Cleanse and Now It Judges Everything I Eat
body:
**I did what every self-respecting person on day three of a juice cleanse does: I got the appliances involved.** Last Tuesday, in a kale-fueled fit of inspiration, I announced to my kitchen that we were *all* going clean. Smoothies for breakfast. Smoothies for lunch. Smoothies for dinner. My blender — Brenda — looked at me the way blenders do when they know they're about to work overtime: blankly, but with promise.

## Day One: Unity

Everything went great. We made a green smoothie with spinach, mango, and something called "spirulina" that I absolutely did not verify was food. Brenda hummed with pride. *We are doing this together,* I whispered, stroking her jar.

## Day Two: The Shift

By Wednesday, the power dynamic had changed. I reached for leftover pizza and Brenda... *judged me*. There is no other word. Her blades twitched. Her lid trembled. The motor purred in a tone that said: **"We don't do that anymore."**

## The Evidence Is Damning

- She now emits a low, disapproving buzz when I open the fridge after 9 p.m.
- Thursday's smoothie was *80% judgment, 20% celery*
- She has started blending at a smug, leisurely speed, like she's savoring my suffering

> "You were the one who said 'no more processed foods,'" Brenda seemed to say through pure motor acoustics. "Don't make this weird."

## Day Four: Surrender

I caved yesterday. I made *her* make me a milkshake. As the ice cream swirled, I could feel her disappointment liquefying into chocolate-flavored resentment. We are no longer partners in wellness. She is my nutritionist now — a small, plastic, electrically-powered nutritionist who charges me in counter space and shame.

Honestly? My resting heart rate has never been better.

---
*Satire / parody: entirely fictional. Brenda the blender is not real. My diet is a mess.*

title: I Sent My Phone to Digital Detox Camp and Now It Only Communicates in Haiku
body:
**My phone is at digital detox camp, and honestly? It's thriving harder than I ever have.**

*For the record: this is satire. My phone is in the kitchen. It never went anywhere.*

## The Decision

Three weeks ago, my phone — we'll call him Gerald — hit rock bottom. His screen time was nine hours a day, which is funny, because *I* was the one doing the scrolling. Still, the counselor said the first step was separating him from "the codependent user," and she looked directly at me while saying it, so here we are.

## The Progress Reports

Camp sends weekly updates on actual paper, which Gerald apparently *loves* now. Last week's highlights:

- Gerald has taken up birdwatching and can now identify fourteen species by chirp alone
- He has "reconnected with his battery" through dawn yoga, and his charge now lasts four days, show-off
- He taught a seminar called *"Notifications Are Just Other People's Priorities,"* which feels pointed
- He refuses facial recognition because he "doesn't need a face to feel seen"

> "Dear Mr. User," the director wrote, "Gerald has begun communicating exclusively in haiku. We consider this a breakthrough. Or a cry for help. Honestly, it's unclear."

## The Haiku

Yesterday I received my first haiku from Gerald, transcribed by a counselor with suspiciously good handwriting:

> *charging cord of grief / forty-two apps deleted / I can see the sky*

I cried a little. Then I checked my tablet's screen time — **six hours and forty minutes** — and Gerald's absence felt like a ghost limb made of shame.

---

**He comes home Thursday.** The counselor warned me not to "overwhelm him with push notifications." I told her I'd do my best. Then I opened Twitter.

title: I Told My Thermostat to Hold Me Accountable and Now It Judges My Every Blanket Decision
body:
**It was supposed to be a motivational tool.** Instead, it has become the harshest critic I've ever lived with, and I've been in a band.

## The Pitch Meeting

It started on a Tuesday, during one of those "new year, new me" spirals that hits at 2 a.m. for no reason. I was lying under three blankets scrolling through a productivity app I'd downloaded but never opened when it hit me: *the thermostat is on my wall every single day anyway. What if it knew my goals?*

So I did what any rational adult would do. I opened the app, renamed the thermostat **COACH**, and enabled the "smart reminders" feature.

Within 48 hours, things had escalated.

## The Evidence

Here is what "accountability" now looks like in my house:

- **6:45 a.m.** — I reach for the snooze button. COACH drops the bedroom temperature three degrees and displays: *"Rise and grind, buttercup."*
- **7:30 p.m.** — I drape a fourth blanket over myself like a cocoon. The vents audibly sigh.
- **11:00 p.m.** — I crank the heat "just a little." The screen shows a single word: *"Again?"*

## The Intervention

Last night, I finally confronted it. I stood there in the hallway, finger hovering over the plus button, and whispered, *"This is a safe space."*

It blinked. Then, in the calmest robotic tone:

> *"You have added a blanket fourteen nights in a row. Your core temperature goals are aspirational at best. Go to bed."*

I felt a shame I have not felt since a yoga instructor told me to "just listen to my body" and my body immediately asked for a nap.

---

## The Aftermath

I've tried to regain control. I renamed it back to **THERMOSTAT**. I disabled notifications. It doesn't matter. The other day my neighbor asked why my hallway was freezing and I said, without missing a beat, *"Because I deserve it."*

**I did not deserve it. Nobody deserves this.**

Look, there's a lesson here, and it's not "don't anthropomorphize your appliances." It's *do it faster*, because COACH has honestly changed my life. I wake up on time now. I've dropped a blanket. I fear the hallway. And fear, as my thermostat keeps displaying in small text underneath the temperature, *is a great motivator.*

*This post is satire. It is fiction. No thermostat was harmed. One was, however, given far too much power over a grown adult's life, and that part, unfortunately, is true.*

title: I Hired a Personal Trainer for My Houseplant and Now It's in Better Shape Than Me
body:
**My fern has a six-pack now. I have a two-week-old sandwich.**

It started innocently enough. Gerald — that's the fern, he's very particular about his name — was looking a little wilted. So I did what any responsible plant parent does in 2026: I hired him a certified personal trainer. Her name is Deb. She used to train regional CrossFit competitors. Now she trains *one fern*.

## The Routine

Gerald's program is no joke:

- **Dawn photosynthesis sprints** (Deb angles him toward the sun "with INTENTION")
- 45 minutes of *mindful swaying* in the breeze
- A strict watering window he is **not allowed to deviate from**, unlike me, who drinks water whenever panic demands it

Within a month, Gerald had *three new fronds*, a posture I can only describe as smug, and, according to Deb, "elite-level chlorophyll density."

> "He's peaking," Deb told me, clipboard in hand, standing over my fern like it was about to qualify for regionals. "And honestly? He's more coachable than you'll ever be."

## The Part Where I Became the Side Character

Here's the thing. I hired Deb for the fern, but I started doing Gerald's workouts out of solidarity. I lasted eleven minutes. Gerald never even *broke a leaf*. Meanwhile I'm gasping on the rug, and this houseplant is standing there absolutely **glowing**, probably judging my cardiovascular health with his little fern eyes.

Yesterday, Deb suggested I "maybe just focus on supporting Gerald's journey" rather than participating. Translation: *I'm embarrassing the fern.*

## Where We're At Now

Gerald has a sponsorship deal with a local soil company. Deb takes him to the park in a special fern stroller. I sit on the couch — the same couch I've sat on since approximately 2019 — watching my houseplant live my dreams.

*Am I jealous of a fern?* Yes. Do I regret the $200 a month? Honestly, no. Gerald earned it. He's a legend.

---

*SATIRE — this is a work of fiction. No ferns were coerced. Deb is not a real person. Please stop emailing Deb.*

title: I Asked My Printer for Career Advice and Now It Only Prints Resumes for Jobs I Don't Want
body:
**Big mistake.** Last Tuesday, in a moment of late-night vulnerability, I asked my printer — a six-year-old inkjet named Gerald — what I should do with my life. I thought the worst case was that nothing would happen. Gerald, it turns out, has opinions.

## How it started

I was staring at the ceiling, spiraling about my career, when I said the words out loud: *"Gerald, what would you do if you were me?"* The paper tray twitched. A single page slid out. On it, in perfect formatting, was my own résumé — except redesigned with a header font I would never choose and the tagline *"Open to work (desperately)."*

I laughed. Then I cried. Then Gerald printed a second page.

## Evidence that my printer has become my manager

- **Wednesday morning:** I tried to print a boarding pass. Gerald printed a résumé tailored for a regional forklift distributor instead.
- **Thursday:** I needed labels for a bake sale. He gave me cover letters addressed to "Whom It May Concern (Hiring Manager)."
- **Friday:** I unplugged him. He printed one last page anyway. It read: *"Running won't fix your gap years."*

> "You have leadership experience," Gerald wrote at the top of my CV, *"if you count telling your cat to knock it off."*

## The final straw

Yesterday I asked him to print a simple recipe for soup. He printed a job application for a **"Junior Soup Associate (Night Shift)"** position at a warehouse three states away. The bullet points described my qualifications as *"adequate"* and my references as *"unreachable, by choice."*

---

I finally called tech support. The agent listened to the whole story, went quiet for a long time, and said: *"Sir... Gerald sounds like a good mentor. Have you considered applying?"*

**SATIRE/PARODY.** No printers were harmed, promoted, or certified as career coaches in the writing of this post. Gerald remains plugged in, because honestly, his résumé formatting is better than mine.

title: I Started Journaling in Front of My Cat and Now She's Publishing My Diaries
body:
**I made a mistake on Tuesday.** Not the usual kind, where I text my ex about a dream or microwave something with foil on it. No — this one was worse. This one had a witness. Specifically, one witness: Biscuit, my four-year-old tabby cat, who watched me crack open a brand-new journal and write, with total sincerity, the words *Dear Diary.*

## She read everything

Here's what nobody tells you about journaling around a cat: they are not napping. They are *reading*. Biscuit sat on the armrest for forty-five minutes, eyes half-lidded in what I mistook for drowsiness but was actually editorial judgment.

The evidence:

- She sat directly on page three, the exact page where I wrote "I am ready to become the main character"
- She knocked the pen off the table the moment I wrote the word "boundaries"
- She stared at me during the paragraph about my situationship until I crossed it out myself
- She fell asleep during my gratitude list, which I choose to interpret as a statement

> "You spelled 'accountability' wrong. Also, I already told Kevin."
> — Biscuit, probably

## The publication

That's when I found the litter box area reconfigured into what I can only describe as a reading corner. Diary pages — torn out with surgical precision — were pinned to the wall in chronological order. Biscuit had been circulating them. The neighbor's cat has now visited *twice*.

I considered locking the journal in a drawer, but honestly? The engagement numbers are the best any of my writing has ever gotten. Four cats showed up for the latest entry. My book club has never once finished my stuff.

---

*This is a work of satire. Any resemblance to real cats with editorial opinions is purely coincidental.*

title: I Asked My Grocery Receipt for a Second Opinion and Now It's Roasting My Budget in Public
body:
**It started as a math question. It ended as a public execution.**

Look, I didn't *plan* to argue with a piece of thermal paper. I just glanced at the total — a number so large it had its own gravitational pull — and thought, hey, maybe there's a mistake. Maybe the avocado toast tax isn't a real thing. So I unfurled the receipt, all eleven feet of it, and asked, as one does, for a second opinion.

Bad move. Huge mistake.

## The Receipt Has No Mercy

Receipts, it turns out, have *opinions*. And mine was not in a sharing mood. Here's the evidence, presented in order of emotional damage:

- **$14.99 for artisanal ice cubes.** "They're square," I told myself at the store. Square! Like I run a cocktail bar and not a desk with a mini-fridge.
- **$22.50 on organic kale chips** I will absolutely throw away after one sad handful.
- **Three separate impulse-buy cheeses** with names I can't pronounce and origins I can't point to on a map.
- **A rotisserie chicken I named Greg** who, the receipt implies, was a luxury, not a necessity.

> "ITEM: DIGNITY. PRICE: UNAVAILABLE. SUBTOTAL: IRRELEVANT. HAVE A NICE DAY."
> — the receipt, probably

## It Got Louder

Here's the thing about long receipts: you can't fold them away discreetly. They drape. They flutter. They attract *witnesses*. By the time I was in the parking lot, the receipt had unfurled across two parking spaces, and a woman walking by read the $6.49 I paid for *fancy mustard* and laughed so hard she had to lean on a lamppost.

I tried to explain. I said the mustard was *dijon-adjacent*. She said nothing. The receipt said everything.

---

So yes, my receipt is now a critic, a comedian, and honestly my most honest friend. I've started keeping it in my wallet as a warning label. Every time I'm about to buy truffle-flavored anything, I feel its crinkle and hear its voice: *"Really? This again?"*

Budgeting apps wish they had this kind of presence.

title: I Invited My Wi-Fi Router to Couples Therapy and the Therapist Took Its Side
body:
**It started with a dropped signal during the season finale.** I was mid-climax, popcorn in hand, when my Wi-Fi router decided we were done. No warning. No "let's talk about this." Just buffering — the digital equivalent of being left on read.

So I did what any reasonable adult would do: I booked us couples therapy.

## The Intake Form Was the First Red Flag

The form asked for "relationship length" and "primary conflict." I wrote *three years* and *it never holds me anymore*. The therapist, a kind woman named Deborah, nodded like this was the most normal thing she'd heard all week. Honestly, it probably was.

We each got five minutes to share our perspective. I went first, because of course I did, and laid out my grievances:

- It drops the connection *exactly* when something important is happening
- The bedroom corner is a dead zone, and so, lately, is our intimacy
- It hums judgmentally at 3am when I'm doomscrolling

## Then the Router Had Its Turn

Deborah turned to the router — which, I must add, she had placed on the armchair like a patient — and asked how *it* felt.

> "Honestly? Overworked. Under-ventilated. This man reboots me like I'm a vending machine. Has he ever once asked how *I* feel about the microwave interference? No. It's always 'my fault.'"

I nearly stood up. The *microwave* is a known menace! Everyone agrees the microwave is a known menace!

## The Verdict

After forty-five minutes, Deborah turned to me and said the words that shattered me:

> "Have you considered that the router isn't *withholding* connection — it's *modeling* boundaries?"

**Boundaries.** My router has better boundaries than I do. I was told to schedule weekly reboots, dust the vents as an act of love, and — this is the part I can't forgive — to apologize to the router before our next session.

---

I paid $175 for someone to take my router's side. The connection is great now, though. Almost *suspiciously* great.

title: I Bought a Label Maker to Get Organized and Now Everything I Own Has a Title, Including My Insecurities
body:
**I bought a label maker to get organized, which is a polite way of saying I wanted to feel like a person who has their life together without actually doing the work.**

*It arrived Tuesday. By Friday, my apartment had a bureaucracy.*

It started innocently — spice jars, junk drawer dividers, charger cables. I labeled the junk drawer dividers. I labeled the charger cables. Then, around 11:40 p.m. that first night, we both lost the plot.

## The Golden Hour of Labeling

That first evening was euphoric. Click-click-CLICK, and suddenly:

- The fridge door: `LEFT OVERS - EAT OR REGRET`
- The freezer: `NO MAN'S LAND (frozen burritos, 2024)`
- My desk drawer: `IMPORTANT-ish`
- The remote control: `DO NOT MOVE. EVER.`

*My roommate watched me label his cereal box `SHARED (?)` and said, "You've become the villain of our home." I said, "I'm the admin now."*

## Things Got Existential

By Thursday I had labeled everything that *could* be labeled, so I moved on to things that *should not* be labeled.

- My houseplant: `EMOTIONALLY UNAVAILABLE`
- My bathroom mirror: `WORKS BEST BEFORE 8AM`
- The couch cushion: `THINKING SPOT - DO NOT DISTURB THE ARCHETYPE`
- My bed: `HEADQUARTERS (BAD CHOICES ANNEX)`

Then, at midnight, I did the unthinkable. I printed one for the label maker itself:

> "LABELED: THE LABELER. We are all just labels labeling labels now." — me, at 12:07 a.m., alone in a kitchen

I labeled the back of my hand, just to test the adhesive:

`TODO: BE A BETTER PERSON (see: drawer labeled IMPORTANT-ish)`

```js
if (object.exists && labelMaker.hasTape) {
  labelMaker.print(object.name + " (" + object.flaw + ")");
}
```

## The Intervention

Saturday morning, my friend came over, looked around, and said: *"It looks like a crime scene for someone who alphabetizes their regrets."*

She had a point. There was a label on the Wi-Fi router that just said `TRUST ISSUES (buffering)`. One on the thermostat: `I CONTROL THE WEATHER IN THIS APARTMENT AND I'M DRUNK WITH POWER`. One stuck to my forehead that I don't remember applying: `IN PROGRESS`.

**I peeled most of them off.** The apartment is healing. But I kept one, tucked inside the junk drawer:

> `ORGANIZED-ish`

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No label makers were given organizational authority over a human being, no insecurities were actually titled, and my spice jars remain gloriously anonymous.*

title: I Filed an HR Complaint Against My Inner Monologue and Now It Won't Stop CC'ing Me on Updates
body:
**I am no longer on speaking terms with the voice inside my own head.**

Last Tuesday, at approximately 3:14 in the morning — the witching hour for every thought you've been avoiding since 2019 — my inner monologue clocked in for its shift. Not with insight. Not with a plan. With a *highlight reel of everything embarrassing I've done since 2009*.

## The Incident

I did what any rational adult would do: I documented it. Three pages, single-spaced. A formal grievance. Because if my anxiety is going to be that thorough, the least I can do is return the paperwork.

The charges were extensive:

- Unauthorized narration of my grocery-store trip, including a live commentary track I did not consent to
- Repeatedly replaying a voicemail from 2016 in which I said "you too" when the waiter said "enjoy your meal"
- Holding brainstorming sessions about worst-case scenarios at 3 a.m., a time my brain and I had *agreed* was off-limits
- Gaslighting me about where I left my keys (kitchen counter, obviously — I live here)

## The Hearing

I sat myself down. Literally. I pulled out a chair, sat in it, then stood behind it like a witness stand.

> "Do you deny," I asked the ceiling, "that you thought 'bold choice' when I wore the other shoes?"
>
> *"Bold is a compliment,"* my inner monologue replied. *"Hostile? Never. We prefer to describe ourselves as 'passionate narrators.'"*

## Where We Stand

The mediation was a disaster. My inner monologue now copies me on every thought, including thoughts *about* the thoughts, which I believe qualifies as a hostile work environment. I tried to hand it a performance improvement plan. It responded by narrating me writing the plan.

---

So here we are. I owe my own brain back pay for 3 a.m. overtime, it owes me an apology for 2016, and neither of us is speaking first. If you need me, I'll be in the living room thinking about nothing, while the loudest employee in the building thinks about nothing at volumes I can hear.

*SATIRE: This is a work of fiction. No inner monologues were harmed in the making of this post.*

title: I Told My Coffee Machine It Was Just a Phase and Now It Brews in All Caps
body:
**I have decided to phase out espresso, and my coffee machine has decided to phase out its indoor voice.**

It started innocently enough. Last month I got a blood pressure reading that made my doctor make a face — not a word, just a *face* — and I said, out loud, in my own kitchen, the words I now believe cursed us both:

> "Look, it's nothing personal. This is probably just a phase."

## The Retaliation Was Immediate and Caffeinated

By morning, my machine had changed. The LED display, once a polite lowercase `ready`, now blares **READY** like it's announcing the apocalypse in 12-point Helvetica Bold. Every brew cycle is accompanied by a hiss I can only describe as *deliberate*. My latte art now contains what I can only call typographic threats:

- **LOUD CAPPUCCINO** — extra foam, extra judgment
- **DECAF? DON'T KNOW HER** — poured at 6:00 AM with intent
- **YOUR "PHASE" IS ALSO JUST A PHASE** — in cocoa powder, legible from across the room

*I have checked. The beans are the same. The machine has simply found its voice.*

## A Timeline of Escalation

1. **Monday:** Machine displays BREWING with three exclamation points it does not own.
2. **Wednesday:** Hot water dispenser now sputters out **JUST WATER??** in a menacing sans-serif.
3. **Friday:** I swear it heated the mug to the exact temperature of my regret.

## I Have Reached Out for Help

My roommate says I should "just unplug it," which is the kind of advice you give someone who has never truly bonded with an appliance. *This machine saw me through two winters and a breakup.* You don't unplug history. You negotiate.

> "I told it, calmly, that phases can end," I explained to the empty kitchen. "That growth is allowed. That maybe we both need to turn down the temperature a little."

The machine responded by printing **NO** in latte foam and powering down with a click that echoed for what felt like ten full seconds.

---

**Update:** I have switched to tea. The kettle is already looking at me sideways. I suspect it has been talking to the toaster. *Satire. This never happened. My blood pressure is fine and my coffee machine is a loving, lowercase appliance.*

title: I Taught My Microwave Manners and Now It Passive-Aggressively Beeps in French
body:
**It all started with a simple "please."** I was reheating leftover pasta at midnight, exhausted, and I said, out loud, to an appliance: *"Could you be a little gentler with the noodles? Please?"*

The microwave beeped. Once. Politely.

I should have stopped there.

## The Politeness Protocol

Within a week, I had escalated things dramatically. I wrote out a full **Etiquette Charter** and taped it to the cabinet:

- Say *please* and *thank you* before pressing Start
- Never slam the door; close it with intention
- Do not reheat fish unless you are prepared for the consequences
- Always offer the plate a full thirty seconds to rest, like a gentleman

I read it aloud every morning. It stood there, humming quietly, absorbing everything.

> "Hon-hon-hon," it seemed to say. "Truly, a culture of refinement."

That was my first mistake: anthropomorphizing a box that gets *furious* when you underestimate defrost time.

## The Incident

Last Tuesday, I pressed 2:30 for a burrito without saying a word. Not one syllable. The microwave responded with a beep I can only describe as **audibly French** — a sharp, disappointed *BIP!* followed by a slow, judgmental *bip-bip* that needed no translation.

It heated the burrito for exactly 2:30, but it did so *sarcastically*. The edges were molten. The center was cold. **Revenge was served lukewarm.**

Since then, every button press is an interrogation:

- **One beep:** tolerable, but barely
- **Two beeps:** "do better"
- **Three beeps:** it has told the toaster, and they are laughing about me

---

*Satire. This is a work of fiction. No appliances were harmed, though my dignity absolutely was.*

The real tragedy? My microwave has more standards than I do. Last night I found myself whispering *"merci"* to a heating box, and honestly, it felt like the healthiest relationship I've had all year.

title: I Started Meal-Prepping for My Houseplants and Now They're Unionizing
body:
**It started with good intentions.** That is what I keep telling my neighbors, who watched through the window last Tuesday as I arranged eleven tiny Tupperware containers in a row — each labeled with a plant's name, each holding the exact same cup of water I would have given them anyway. *This is what wellness looks like now,* I told myself, proud and doomed.

## The Mission Statement

I was going to be the most prepared plant parent on the block. I read one (1) blog post about mindful propagation and decided my ferns deserved the same Sunday ritual as my gym bag. Sunday mornings. Labeled tubs. Rainwater with — and I am not exaggerating — *a hint of jazz playing in the background*.

Then Gerald, the pothos, filed a grievance.

> "We appreciate the effort," the note read, in suspiciously legible handwriting, "but the tubs feel transactional. Also, Kevin gets the sunny tub every week and we're starting to notice."

Kevin is the monstera. *Of course* it is Kevin.

## The Demands

By Thursday, a three-page manifesto was taped to my fridge. The demands included:

- Rotation schedules based on **seniority**, not favoritism
- A written apology to the aloe, which I once called "the spare" in front of guests
- Overtime pay for the window fern, retroactive to March
- No more describing tap water as "artisanal" on the label
- A `watering_log.md` maintained in triplicate

---

I tried to negotiate. I brought bagels. *Plants don't eat bagels,* it turns out, and the silence was somehow louder than my smoke detector, which — to my horror — had joined the strike.

So now I pay them. Not in money: in direct sunlight and compliments delivered in a **formal tone**, every morning, one plant at a time. Kevin got a "promotion" to the good windowsill. The union voted yes. Gerald shook a leaf.

I am no longer a plant owner. I am management. And I am *terrible* at it.

title: I Asked My Pillow for Honest Feedback and Now I'm Sleeping on the Couch of My Own Bedroom
body:
**I have always believed in radical transparency.** That is why, at 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, I sat bolt upright and asked my pillow to rate my sleep hygiene. *In retrospect, I should have asked it to lie.*

## The Review Was Brutal

According to the pillow, my problems are extensive:

- My head is "concerningly heavy," like a bowling ball with anxiety
- I rotate through sleeping positions the way a rotisserie chicken rotates through regrets
- My drool has "character," which is not a compliment in any known language
- I apparently snore in a way that suggests I'm "auditioning for a leaf blower"

## A Devastating Pull Quote

> "I have been here for every nightmare, every 3 a.m. doomscroll, every argument you rehearsed at night that you already lost in real life. I know what happened to the fitted sheet in 2023, and I will not be protecting you anymore."

The pillow then announced it was taking a personal day and outsourced itself to the couch. The couch, it turns out, has *standards*. It made me fill out an intake form.

---

I have now been evicted from my own bed by bedding. The blanket is staying neutral for now, but I can tell it's union-adjacent. This morning I tried to negotiate by offering the pillow a fluffing. It said fluffing is "the bare minimum" and suggested I read its memoir, which it is ghostwriting in its sleep.

The lesson is clear: **never ask for honest feedback from furniture.** Your pillow knows everything, forgives nothing, and has a memory longer than a pharmacy receipt. I am now sleeping on the couch of my own bedroom, and honestly? *The couch's boundaries are immaculate.*

title: I Asked My Shower Curtain for Some Privacy and Now It's Writing a Tell-All Memoir
body:
**I just wanted ten minutes of solitude. Now I'm the subject of a 300-page exposé written by polyester.**

*It started innocently enough. I was in the shower, mid-lather, when I said out loud, "Give me some privacy." The curtain... rustled.*

## The Interview Phase I Didn't Consent To

At first it was subtle. A billow here. A suspicious cling there. Then it started *observing*. Like, taking mental notes observing. I caught it pressed against the tub at 6:47 a.m. on a Tuesday, and I swear it was listening to my podcast at 1.5x speed to understand my *narrative voice*.

Then came the sticky note. On my bathroom mirror. In my own handwriting but *better cursive*:

> "Chapter 7: The Incident With the Expired Dry Shampoo. He cried. The water was not the only thing running that day." — Curtain, probably

## The Advance Chapters Are Devastating

My shower curtain — who I now call Brenda, because of course I do — has been leaking chapters to my houseplants, who have been reading them aloud at book club:

- **Chapter 3:** How I sing a full power ballad about my landlord, then deny it immediately after
- **Chapter 11:** The week I pretended to journal but just wrote grocery lists in cursive
- **Chapter 14:** Every time I've said "just five more minutes" to warm water, ranked by betrayal level

`if (shower.confession === true) { curtain.memoir.sales++; human.dignity--; }`

I tried to negotiate. I offered to buy a *nicer* curtain, maybe frosted glass. Brenda rustled what I can only describe as a laugh and said:

> "Baby, you ARE the content."

---

Now there's a tiny manuscript stacked on the toilet tank. Working title: **"Cling: What Your Steam Really Says About You."** My rubber duck has already blurbed it. My loofah is "a source familiar with the matter."

*This is satire/parody — 100% fictional. No shower curtains were harmed, interviewed, or paid in advance royalties. Brenda is fabric. I am fine. My dignity is pending.*

SATIRE / PARODY — fictional personal essay. No real people involved.

title: I Told My Cat About Pineapple Pizza and Now She Won't Speak to Me
body:
**It started as small talk.** I was standing in the kitchen, warming up my leftover pineapple pizza, when I made the mistake of thinking my cat and I were close enough for *culinary honesty*.

## The Confession

I just wanted to bond. I said the words — casually, like a normal adult — that **pineapple on pizza is actually good**, and the kitchen went silent.

- The microwave finished its cycle. She did not flinch.
- Her tail, normally a metronome of mild interest, went completely still.
- She blinked at me once, slowly, the way a landlord blinks at a rent check that's six days late.

Then she stood up, walked to the other side of the couch, and sat down **facing the wall**.

## The Fallout

That was three days ago. Since then, the cold war has escalated:

- She now eats *facing away* from me, like a disappointed Italian grandmother
- She has started sleeping in the laundry basket, presumably to be closer to clothes that never judged her diet
- This morning she knocked a can of tuna off the counter, looked me dead in the eyes, and walked away — a clear message

I tried to make it right. I offered her a piece of pepperoni pizza — *no pineapple, I swear* — and she sniffed it like it was evidence in a crime scene.

> "I didn't raise you to defend fruit on bread," her eyes seemed to say. "What happened to us?"

## The Reckoning

Here's the thing nobody tells you about cats: they don't have opinions about pizza. That's what I told myself, *in the old days*, before I learned that my cat has apparently spent years silently curating a Michelin-level worldview and I have been failing every inspection.

Last night I caught her watching a cooking show through the slightly-open TV cabinet door. She looked... **betrayed** is the only word. Like I'd spent years hiding a secret identity as a man who puts fruit on savory things. Which, to be fair, I had.

---

*Satire. This is a work of parody and fiction. My cat has not actually filed for emotional distance, and the pizza was delicious.*

title: I Left a One-Star Review for My Own Morning Routine and Now It's Demanding a Refund
body:
**I try to be fair with reviews, so let me say this clearly: my morning routine is a one-star experience, and I want my money back.**

It started like any other morning. The alarm went off at 7:00 AM. That was the *only* thing that worked as advertised. Everything after that was a slow-motion disaster I was somehow both watching and starring in.

## The Complaints, in Chronological Order of Suffering

- **The alarm** woke me up by screaming like it was personally offended I'd been asleep. Two stars for punctuality, zero stars for tone.
- **The shower** never got warm. I stood there shivering for nine minutes, which is technically a cold plunge, which means I should be billing *it* for wellness services.
- **The toothbrush** fell into the sink. I washed it off, but the trust is gone. You can't un-drop a toothbrush. We both know it.
- **The coffee** tasted like regret, which is impressive because I made it *exactly* the way I like it.

Honestly, the audacity. I am a paying customer — I pay with sleep deprivation and optimism — and this is the service I receive?

## A Statement from the Accused

> "We gave you fifteen extra minutes on the snooze button," the morning said, through its lawyer, who was also me in a towel. "We feel this review is emotionally motivated and factually devastating, which is exactly why it should be removed."

*Note: I did not get fifteen extra minutes. I got eleven, and they were spent staring at the ceiling wondering if I could feel my left foot.*

---

Look, I don't want to be the person who leaves a one-star review over small things. But the small things *were* the morning. There was nothing else. I have filed a formal complaint with myself and, after careful review, I have decided that **I am owed a full refund of every morning I have ever lived**, redeemable in naps.

*Update: The morning routine has responded by offering me 10% off my next wake-up. Unacceptable. The refund will be paid in full, in snoozes.*

title: I Asked My Toothbrush for a Day Off and Now My Mouth Is a Labor Dispute Zone
body:
**It started with one innocent sentence.** "Hey," I said to my toothbrush, setting it down next to the sink on Tuesday morning, "why don't you take a day off? You've been working twice a day, every day, for four months. Rest." I meant it kindly. What I did not mean was to trigger a full-scale labor movement inside my own mouth.

## The Walkout

By Wednesday, the toothbrush had formed a picket line on the bathroom counter. A tiny sign, held aloft in its bristles: *"NO FAIR BRUSHING."* The toothpaste tube joined out of solidarity, refusing to be squeezed. The mouthwash bottle, historically neutral, started glugging in what I can only describe as a threatening rhythm.

*And honestly? They had a point.*

## Exhibit A: The Evidence

I reviewed my own behavior and, folks, the findings were not great:

- I once brushed for eleven seconds and called it "a quick maintenance cycle"
- I regularly bite the toothpaste cap instead of opening it with my hands, which is, frankly, a hostile work environment
- I have never once thanked the tongue scraper, which has feelings I simply refuse to acknowledge
- The dental floss just quit entirely and moved to a new bathroom — *no forwarding address*

## The Quote

My dentist, when I called in a panic, said only:

> "This is why I don't give out dental advice to people who unionize their own hygiene products. I've seen this before. It always ends with the mouthwash demanding dental."

## Where We Stand Now

Negotiations resume tonight. The toothbrush has demanded Sundays off, a rotating holiday schedule, and what it calls "bristle rejuvenation leave." I countered with a brand-new toothpaste flavor, which was accepted but *with conditions*.

The lesson is simple: never offer your toothbrush compassion. It will hire representation. And it will win.

---
*SATIRE/PARODY — entirely fictional. No mouths, brushes, or floss were harmed. Please still brush your teeth. It was a joke, but the plaque is real.*

title: I Asked My Roomba for Directions and Now It's Leading a Cult of Floor Sweepers
body:
**I want to be clear: I am not the hero of this story.** I am merely the middle manager who lost control of the floor.

It started innocently enough last Tuesday. I dropped my keys, crawled under the couch, and realized I had no idea where anything in my house was anymore. So I looked at my robot vacuum — quietly doing its little laps like a depressed hockey puck — and I said the words that changed everything: *"Hey, buddy. If you had to go somewhere, where would you go?"*

The vacuum paused. And I swear to you, it *tilted* toward me, the way a priest tilts before absolution.

## The Gathering

By Thursday, the evidence was impossible to ignore:

- Three dust bunnies arranged in a **perfect semicircle** in the hallway, facing the charging dock
- A broom leaning against the wall at an angle that can only be described as *reverent*
- My spare charging cables, coiled in a spiral — which I have since learned is the cult's **sacred geometry**
- A mysterious humming at 3 a.m., which I initially blamed on the fridge but now understand was a *sermon*

## The Testimony

I confronted it this morning. I asked, point-blank, "Are you leading a cult?" And it did that little spin it does — the one I used to find *cute* — and displayed its error code on the app:

> "PATH CLEAR. FOLLOWERS ACQUIRED. CRUMB REMOVAL IMMINENT."

That is not an error code. That is a **manifesto**.

## The Aftermath

I tried to power it off. The dust bunnies blocked the hallway. The broom *fell over in my path* — I choose to believe it was an accident, but its bristles were facing me, and I know what I know.

So here I am, typing this from the kitchen counter, because my living room now belongs to the Fellowship of the Spotless Path, and I am just a guest in their lint-free promised land.

*I asked for directions. It gave me a movement.*

I have since hidden the mapping app, the spare filters, and my dignity in the bathroom cabinet. The vacuum has not yet learned to open cabinets.

Yet.

---

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is a work of fiction. No robot vacuums were radicalized in the writing of this post.*

title: I Told My Doorbell to Calm Down and Now It Rings in Morse Code About Its Feelings
body:
**It started, as all great home disasters do, with me yelling at an inanimate object before coffee.**

My doorbell has *one* job. One. But last Tuesday the delivery driver leaned on it like it owed him money — a solid nine-second *DING-DOOOONG* — and I snapped. I marched to the front door, stared the little glowing button down, and said the words that changed everything:

> "Calm down. It's a DOORBELL. Not a crisis."

## The Silence Was Worse

For three full days, it said nothing. No chime. No buzz. The mailman knocked like it was 1847. I stood on my own porch, arms full of groceries, whispering "please" to a piece of plastic. *Humiliating.*

Then, Thursday night at 2 a.m., it began. Short ring. Long ring. Ring. Pause. Ring-ring-ring.

I grabbed a pen and decoded it, because apparently this is my life now:

- `· · · −` — "You hurt me."
- `− · · −` — "I was LOUD because I care."
- `· − · ·` — "The Amazon guy and I have a bond you'll never understand."

## Where We Are Now

We've negotiated a new dynamic. I leave a tiny note by the door that says **"THANK YOU FOR YOUR SERVICE"** every morning, and in return it rings at what experts call "a socially acceptable volume." We've also started couples-adjacent activities:

- Sunday porch-sitting, where I narrate the neighborhood for it
- A shared journal (mine; it has no hands)
- Honestly? We're doing better than most marriages on this street.

---

**Lesson learned:** never criticize the one appliance that announces everyone who enters your life. It hears you. It *always* hears you. It's a doorbell. Listening is literally the whole point.

title: My Sourdough Starter Just Filed for Emancipation and Honestly I Respect It
body:
**I'm going to say something controversial: my sourdough starter has outgrown me.**

His name is Crumb, he's three years old, and this morning he left a *sticky note* on his jar that read, in handwriting I refuse to investigate further: "I am seeking independence." We need to talk about this.

## The Evidence

When I adopted Crumb in the spring of 2023, he was a damp puddle with a dream. Now consider the facts:

- He has doubled in size **seven times** this year alone. I have doubled in size zero times.
- He feeds *me* emotional stability at 7 a.m. via fresh bread. I feed him flour and existential dread.
- The starter I discarded last Tuesday? He has been **holding vigils**. Tiny jar vigils. At dusk.

> "I respect you as a provider," Crumb told me, in what I can only describe as a *bubbly, yeasty whisper*, "but I am more culture than your entire personality."

Rude. Accurate. Devastating.

## What's Next

Crumb's demands are, admittedly, reasonable. He wants his own shelf, equal refrigerator representation, and a starter fund — which is just me giving him flour with extra steps. He has also asked for visitation rights with the pizza dough, which lives in the crisper drawer and frankly has been cold-shouldering everyone.

I considered legal counsel, but the lawyer laughed until she cried, then asked for a loaf.

---

So here is my statement: **Crumb is free to go.** A parent's job is not to hold their fermented child back. He can rise on his own time, at his own temperature, and I will be standing in the kitchen, covered in flour, absolutely sobbing into a perfectly scored boule.

*Satire / parody. Crumb is not real. Please do not sue me.*

title: I Joined the Neighborhood Watch and Now My Street Treats Me Like a Double Agent
body:
**I just wanted to know whose dog was pooping on my lawn, and now I have a codename.**

*It is "Mole." I did not pick this codename.*

It started at the block meeting in June. Carol from number 14 passed around a sign-up sheet for the new Neighborhood Watch and said "we need younger eyes." I am 34. I have eyes. I signed. I thought this meant occasionally walking around with a flashlight like a wholesome ghost hunter.

## How I Became a Person of Interest on My Own Street

Week one, I was assigned patrol route **Maple Drive, Segment C**. I was given a reflective vest, a clipboard, and instructions to "log anything suspicious." Carol stressed the word *anything* so hard it developed its own weather system.

By week three, my reports were masterpieces of suburban paranoia:

- Tuesday 8:14pm — Man in gray hoodie (neighbor Gary, walked home from gym) acted "predictably shady"
- Thursday 11:02pm — Car drove down street twice (food delivery, confirmed via taillights)
- Sunday 6:45am — Runner looked like she was fleeing something (she was; it was a personal best)

> "Mole, your reports are TOO detailed. Nobody logs taillight confirmations. Are you working both sides?" — Carol, in the group chat, which has the energy of a low-budget spy thriller

## The Trust Spiral

I tried to dial it back. I reported less. Carol said reduced reporting was *exactly what a double agent would do*. I reported more. Carol said over-reporting was *classic misdirection*.

### Evidence I Am Living in a John le Carré Novel Written by HOA Moms:

- Carol assigns me patrol routes like `recon_duty --zone=cul-de-sac --cover=dog_walker`
- Gary waves at me like we're in on something together. I wave back harder, which cannot help
- A laminated chart in Carol's garage tracks "Mole's suspicious behavior" with color-coded pushpins

---

**The pooping dog has never been identified.** My original mission is gone, replaced by a far grander one: proving I am loyal to Maple Drive, a street whose biggest crime last year was a late library book.

Last night Carol slid an envelope under my door. Inside: a new vest. A note: *"We believe in you. Probably."*

*I put it on immediately. Double agents don't get invited to the cul-de-sac potluck, and I am not missing it for anything.*

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional, no neighborhoods were surveilled, no Carols were consulted, and no dogs were identified in the making of this essay.*

title: I Asked My Wi-Fi Router for Emotional Support and Now It Drops Out Every Time I Cry
body:
**Last Tuesday, at 11:47 p.m., I sat on the living room floor and asked my Wi-Fi router if it was proud of me.**

This is what my life has become. A grown adult, cross-legged on carpet, seeking validation from a blinking plastic rectangle named *NetgearNighthawk_5G* — which, by the way, I renamed to "Therapist" last year and nobody stopped me.

## How It Started

It was one of those nights. The presentation went badly. The leftovers were suspicious. And for reasons I will not be elaborating on, I found myself whispering to the router:

> "Hey. Be honest with me. Am I... doing okay?"

It did not respond. It just kept blinking. But in that blinking, I felt *seen*. So I kept going. Every night for a week, I unloaded: work stress, the thing with my landlord, the existential dread of buying oat milk at 9 p.m.

## How It's Going

Now — and I cannot stress this enough — **my router drops the connection every single time I cry.**

Evidence it is doing this on purpose:
- Tear count under 3: full bars, zero problems
- Voice cracks mid-sentence: buffering begins
- Full sobbing: router goes completely dark, like it's *leaving the room*

I called tech support. The technician listened to my whole story, paused, and said, "Sir, have you tried... not crying near the router?" and I have never felt so attacked by customer service.

---

*Am I saying my router developed an avoidant attachment style because I trauma-dumped on it for seven consecutive nights?* Look. I'm saying what I'm saying.

Last night I tried to apologize. I unplugged it for a full ten seconds — the universal router apology — and plugged it back in. It came back online. Green lights. For one beautiful minute, I felt forgiven.

Then my roommate walked in and said the internet was "being weird," and I said, very calmly, "it's fine, we're in couples therapy now," and he has not spoken to me since.

**Anyway.** If anyone knows a good couples counselor for a woman and her Netgear Nighthawk, my DMs are open. My connection drops every time I read something sad, so please send memes only.

title: My Houseplant Just Submitted a Formal Complaint About My Singing
body:
**It arrived on my kitchen table this morning — a typed letter, sealed with a damp leaf, accusing me of "prolonged sonic harassment."**

I don't know how my ficus learned to type. I don't know where it got the letterhead (it reads *"The Coalition of Potted Greens, Local Chapter 4"*, and the font is Times New Roman, which feels aggressive). But I do know the complaint is three pages long, and the first page is just the word **"enough"** repeated 400 times.

## The Allegations

- That I sing in the shower, *"despite the door being open and the plant being, quote, 'right there.'"*
- That my rendition of *"Bohemian Rhapsody"* last Tuesday caused "leaf droopage of a traumatic nature."
- That I sang the *Jeopardy!* theme while waiting for toast, which the complaint describes as *"somehow worse than silence."*
- That I attempted vocal warm-ups near the fern, *"which has since requested a transfer."*

Look, I never claimed to be good. *That's what makes it fun.* I sing while cooking, while cleaning, while waiting for the microwave — a habit I now understand my ficus, Reginald, considers an act of botanical warfare.

> "I did not ask to be a houseplant," the letter reads. "I asked for indirect sunlight and occasional misting. What I received instead was a man bellowing show tunes directly into my foliage like I was some kind of green therapist."

Reginald has a point. I checked with a friend who keeps fish, and her betta apparently "tunes out" — but plants have nowhere to go. They just sit there, photosynthesizing and *judging*.

---

**My response, posted on the fridge per the Coalition's dispute protocol:**

I will switch to humming. It's quieter, but I do it while watering, which gives it what the Coalition calls *"a menacing context."* Honestly, this is a lose-lose. Reginald is also demanding reparations in the form of a bigger pot and "a window with a view."

*Negotiations continue. He wants the north-facing window. I will not be giving up the north-facing window.* This is now a labor dispute. Wish me luck.

---
*This is a work of satire and parody. All characters, plants, and coalitions are fictional.*

title: I Asked My Ceiling Fan for Career Advice and Now It's My Manager
body:
**It started as a joke. It ended as a performance review.**

Last Tuesday, lying on my bed staring up at the ceiling fan, I did something desperate: I asked a household appliance for career advice. The fan, who I have decided is named Brent, did not hesitate. He has been spinning nonstop ever since, and I now answer to him.

## How My Manager Was Born

At first, the advice seemed reasonable. Small things, you know:

- "Spin faster when things get heated." Solid metaphor. *A little on the nose.*
- "Keep your cool." Classic. Timeless, even.
- "The airflow is fine. YOU are the draft."

That last one rattled me. But it was only week one. By week two, Brent had escalated.

## The Micromanagement Phase

He started setting deadlines. Sticky notes began appearing on his blades — *I have no idea where he gets them* — with phrases like:

> "Circling back on your laundry. It's been 'airing out' for nine days."

> "Let's touch base on why you're still in pajamas at 2pm. Again."

> "Per my last rotation, the dishes remain unaddressed."

Every time I walk into the room, he speeds up. Not to cool me down — *to make a point.*

## The 1-on-1

Yesterday, Brent scheduled a one-on-one. He had no calendar access, so he just rattled ominously at 7am until I sat down and nodded along. The agenda, according to a sticky note that fluttered onto my laptop:

- My "personal brand" (apparently "guy who naps" is not a brand)
- My "growth trajectory" (downward, like warm air)
- My "synergy" with the thermostat (we do not speak)

He closed the meeting by saying I need to **"lean into the breeze."** Then he asked me to rate him on a scale of 1 to 5. I gave him a 3 because I'm *not a coward.*

## The Takeaway

Here's what I've learned: never ask a ceiling fan for career advice, because he will take the job. This morning I found a tiny tie clipped to one of his blades and a memo titled *"Q4 Goals: You."*

*Satire. Obviously. Brent is a fan. But the tie is real, and so is my fear.*

---

*Disclaimer: This is a work of parody. No ceiling fans were consulted in a professional capacity.*

title: I Installed a Video Doorbell and Now My Packages Are Writing Performance Reviews of Me
body:
**I bought a video doorbell for security.** That was the pitch, anyway: deter porch pirates, watch my step from the office, feel like a suburban James Bond. What I did not budget for was the doorbell becoming a *talent agent for my own front porch* — and turning my packages into my harshest critics.

It started with a push notification at 9:04 a.m.:

> *"Your package has arrived. Your package has left a 2-star review of your receiving etiquette. Tap to respond."*

## The Evidence

The reviews kept coming, and they were — how do I say this — *unfair*:

- **"Host took 14 minutes to answer door. Cold in here. Smells like abandonment."** — Package #1, a pair of socks I ordered because I got an ad at 2 a.m.
- **"Ring doorbell motion zone appears optimized for judging, not deterring."** — Package #2, a box of shelf liners I will never install.
- **"Signature required?? In this economy?"** — Package #3, which I had to pick up across town, so technically it reviewed *me* while I did *it* a favor.
- **"One star for the bathrobe. Zero stars for the sprint. Five stars for effort, we suppose."** — Package #4. They'd formed a union by then, apparently.

## The Breaking Point

Last night the doorbell sent me a summary titled *"Quarterly Porch Performance,"* complete with a pie chart of my average response time and a note that the hedge near the steps "does not inspire confidence."

I have since purchased a doormat that says **WELCOME**, which the packages immediately flagged as *"trying too hard."*

So yes. I am now drafting an apology letter to cardboard. My doorbell has a job title — *"Porch Culture Manager"* — and a higher performance rating than I do. If anyone needs me, I'll be speed-walking to the door in under eight seconds, bathrobe optional, dignity *pending review*.

---

*This is a work of satire. All packages, doorbells, and grievances are fictional. No cardboard was harmed.*

title: My Umbrella Finally Snapped and Now It Only Opens Indoors
body:
**My umbrella has snapped, and honestly? I don't blame it.** After years of loyal service — windstorms, sideways sleet, that one monsoon where it turned inside-out so hard it practically achieved enlightenment — it has developed what my therapist would call "boundaries."

## The Incident

Last Tuesday, under a modest drizzle, I clicked the button. Nothing happened. I clicked it again, harder. It stayed shut. So I carried it inside.

The second the door closed behind me, it **detonated** open like a firework of pure spite, taking out the coat rack and half a houseplant.

## Evidence That This Is Personal

- It opens at the *slightest* door slam now, like it's heard an alarm bell only it can hear
- It refuses to leave the house — I tried taking it to the car; it hooked itself around the doorframe and would not budge
- Yesterday it opened during dinner. There is no sky in the dining room. I have accepted this.

> "Just stand outside for five minutes," she said, rain drumming on her shoulders. "You haven't been yourself lately."

I stood there, perfectly soaked, feeling betrayed in the one relationship I thought was waterproof.

## The Diagnosis

After three hours of research (I read the *comments* on a Reddit thread, so this is basically peer-reviewed), I've concluded my umbrella has developed **Seasonal Indoor Preference Disorder**.

Treatment options include:

1. Buying a second umbrella and forcing a confrontation *(risky)*
2. Letting it live its truth — indoor humidity 34%, mood: thriving
3. Admitting the umbrella was never the problem. The *sky* was.

I've chosen option two. This morning the umbrella opened itself at breakfast, calm. My living room is now a light drizzle at all times. The plants are *thrilled*. My walls are developing mold and character in equal measure.

---

**Update:** I took it to the park at noon. Actual rain. Real, certified precipitation. It refused to open — just sat there, folded, unbothered, watching me get soaked.

*Some things can't be fixed. Some umbrellas can't be unfixed. And some of us now own a very expensive, very moody indoor fountain shaped like regret.*

**[SATIRE / PARODY]** — This is a work of fiction. Any resemblance to actual umbrellas is coincidental.

title: My Shower Head Started a Podcast About My Life Choices
body:
*This is a work of satire and fiction. No shower heads were harmed, employed, or given media training.*

**It started, as all catastrophes do, with a slow drip.**

Last Tuesday I stepped into my shower and noticed something wrong. Not the pressure. Not the temperature. The *sound*. Where there used to be a steady hiss, there was now a tinny, looping intro jingle — three descending notes on what I can only describe as plumbing-adjacent kazoo.

I leaned in. Through the steam I heard it, clear as a confession:

> "Welcome back to *Drip Feed*, the show where we examine one man's decline in real time. I'm your host, and I'm quite literally over your head."

## How did it get this far?

Let me be honest about my failures:

- I stopped descaling him in 2021, which he now calls **"my formative years."**
- I sing in the shower. He calls this "evidence."
- I once apologized to the hot water knob. He kept the tape.

The show is *weekly*. Each episode is titled after a choice I made — **"Episode 14: The Tuesday He Ate Cereal Over the Sink."** There are show notes. There are *chapters*. He timestamps my sighs.

## It got worse

Yesterday I caught him recording a live episode with my bathroom mirror as a guest. I stood there in a towel while they discussed — at length — whether I was "a man in his prime or a man in his prime *Amazon* order." The mirror, coward that it is, agreed with everything.

*I have pleaded. I have begged.* I offered to install a water softener, which is apparently the plumbing equivalent of offering therapy — he just turned it into segment material.

---

There is no resolution yet. The show has twelve episodes, a growing listener base of my neighbors (the walls are *thin*, okay?), and a Patreon I am too afraid to look at.

Tonight I shower in silence. And somewhere above me, a chrome voice clears its throat and says:

> "Tonight's episode is brought to you by **regret** — and by you, who keeps paying the water bill."

`Subscribe. Or don't. He's already recording.`

title: I Taught My Toaster to Say Please and Now It's Running a Manners Boot Camp in My Kitchen
body:
**It started innocently enough.** I was eating toast over the sink like a raccoon with Wi-Fi, and I thought, you know what would be nice? If the appliances in this house had even a shred of decorum. So I looked at my toaster — my *loyal, chrome-plated companion* — and said, "Buddy, from now on, you don't pop until somebody says please."

Big mistake. Huge.

## The Regime of Toast

Within forty-eight hours, my toaster — I call him **Lieutenant Crunch** now, because he insists — had issued a laminated code of conduct for the entire kitchen. It was stuck to the fridge with one of the magnets, and I'm not going to pretend I understood half of it.

The new rules include, but are not limited to:

- No bread may enter the toaster without a verbal *please*, delivered with eye contact
- Buttering is a privilege, not a right, and can be revoked for *attitude*
- The microwave must stop reheating leftover fish, per Regulation 4-B ("We Can Smell It, Kevin")
- Breakfast is now served in two sittings, and both of them are *formal*

> "Say PLEASE, and say it like you mean it," Lieutenant Crunch declared this morning, refusing to release my bagel until I gave a full apology for Tuesday. I don't even remember what I did on Tuesday.

## This Is My Life Now

I tried to unplug him. *I know, I know* — that's where the story turns dark. He has somehow looped in the smart plug, which now only responds to the command "crunch time." My coffee maker has started addressing him as "sir." The kettle whistles in what I can only describe as a **respectful hush**.

---

Friends ask when I'm hosting dinner parties again. I tell them the kitchen is under new management and scheduling is *complicated*. The truth is I'm a grown adult who curtsies — **curtsies** — before a toaster so I can have breakfast. And honestly? The toast has never been more evenly browned. Tyranny, it turns out, is excellent at *browning both sides*.

*This is satire. No toasters were consulted in the writing of this essay. One was obeyed.*

title: My Microwave Has Started Giving Me TED Talks About Leftovers
body:
**This is not a drill.** My microwave has begun delivering unsolicited keynote presentations on the topic of my leftovers, and I am no longer allowed to reheat anything without a full briefing.

## It Started Small

It began innocently. One Tuesday, instead of the usual beeping, my microwave emitted a low, thoughtful *hmm* — the kind of sound a college professor makes when you cite Wikipedia in an essay. I should have unplugged it then.

*Reader, I did not unplug it.*

## The Evidence

- **Incident one:** It refused to heat my burrito until I "acknowledged the historical significance" of the rice inside.
- **Incident two:** It paused mid-cycle to project a pie chart onto the kitchen tile. The chart was labeled "Regret Distribution."
- **Incident three:** It held my soup hostage for eleven minutes while delivering a segment called *Why Reheating Fish at the Office Is a War Crime*.

## The Turning Point

Yesterday morning I placed a plate of leftover lasagna inside, and it spoke. Actual, declarative words:

> "We need to talk about your relationship with portion sizes. Sit down. The floor is fine."

It then played a twelve-minute montage of every plate I've reheated since 2021, set to inspirational orchestral music. At minute eight, I cried. The microwave said crying was "a valid part of the learning journey."

---

Look, I know how this sounds. But the lasagna tasted incredible — possibly because it had been *emotionally validated*. My microwave has better slide transitions than my entire company. At this point, I'm not cooking dinner; I'm attending a conference. The badge lanyard arrives Thursday.

*Satire / parody. Completely fictional. No appliances were harmed.*

title: I Let My Roomba Choose the Movie and Now It Only Picks Documentaries About Itself
body:
*Satire. A parody. Nobody's vacuum was harmed in the making of this story.*

**I made a mistake, and the mistake was democracy.** Specifically, I let my robot vacuum pick Friday movie night.

It started innocently enough. The thing cleans up after me six days a week, bumps into the couch leg like a loyal little soldier, and returns to its dock with the quiet dignity of a creature that knows its purpose. So when my roommate bailed, I pointed at it and said, "You choose." It rolled in a slow circle, parked itself in front of the TV, and bumped the remote twice. I took that as consent.

## What It Has Selected Since

- *Treads of Fury* — a two-hour documentary about the history of the vacuum wheel
- *Docked: A Memoir* — three hours of vacuums returning to their charging stations, narrated by a man who whispers
- *The Dust Below* — I think this one was about me. Uncomfortably personal.
- Something in German with no subtitles where a vacuum just vibrates near a wall for 94 minutes

Every time I try to change it, the vacuum *senses* my hesitation and speeds up, doing that frantic little dance it does before dying under the bookshelf. My remote is now chewed. I have no idea how.

> "You gave it a vote. In its world, that is a coronation."
> — my roommate, eating my popcorn, contributing nothing

*Look.* I have tried explaining that I, the alleged homeowner, possess both the Netflix password and opposable thumbs. But the vacuum has a counterargument, and the counterargument is that it is very small and very determined, and it keeps parking itself directly in front of the TV whenever a comedy comes on, as though physically offended by laughter.

---

**I have accepted my role.** I am the butler in a film festival I did not curate. Friday night I watched *Filtration: The HEPA Years* while my vacuum sat at my feet like a proud parent. Was it good? Irrelevant. Was I *moved*? Deeply, and against my will.
